The article examines the features, priority goals, and risks of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into medical education. The work examines how future doctors implement digital tools in their training and assess their role in future practice. A survey of 79 4th and 6th year students of the Ternopil National Medical University named after I. Ya. Horbachevsky, who study “Obstetrics and Gynecology”, revealed a paradox. On the one hand, AI has become a part of daily routine for 67.1 % of respondents, another 31.6 % turn to it several times a week. The main advantage is the optimization of time spent: 97.5 % of respondents confirmed significant resource savings. However, the implementation is superficial, as 100 % rely on general-purpose text language models (ChatGPT, Claude) rather than specialized medical software. Expert assistants (UpToDate, Glass AI) are integrated by only 8.9 % of respondents, and image generation programs by 6.3 %. It was found that 83.5 % of students turn to AI to search for clinical protocols; 67.1 % to prepare for the KROK/OSKI exams; 67.1 % to solve clinical problems or write case histories, and only 17.7 % to translate articles. An important aspect was the analysis of self-assessment of prompting skills on a 5-point scale: 12.7 % of students rated them 5 points, 36.7 % rated them 4 points, 46.8 % rated them 3 points, and 3.8 % rated them 2 points. Despite high confidence, 93.7 % of respondents personally encountered AI “hallucinations” – the generation of non-existent facts. Future doctors are clearly aware of the risks of degradation of clinical thinking (63.3 %, n = 50), getting used to “easy answers” (65.3 %, n = 52), and unconscious assimilation of false information (43.0 %, n = 34). The introduction of mandatory discipline in medical AI was fully supported by 23.4 % (n = 18) of respondents, actively supported with reservations by 18.2 % (n = 14), and taken in a neutral position by 45.5 % (n = 35). Based on the data obtained, it is concluded that medical students demonstrate a high intensity of AI use against the background of a critical shortage of work with profile software and a high frequency of encounters with neural network errors. The results justify the need for a strategic transformation of higher medical education – a transition from ignoring technology to the implementation of systematic training in medical prompting, data verification methodology, and digital hygiene for the safe use of AI in future practice.

documents.abstract: This article examines the impacts of generative artificial intelligence on digital game design creation, investigating how this technology transforms creative processes in the industry. The research, using a qualitative approach, employed bibliographic review, comparative case study between Palworld and Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, and semi-structured interviews with three professionals in the field. The analysis identified five thematic categories: technological democratization, transformation of creative processes, preservation of human authenticity, ethical issues, and professional adaptation. The results show that generative AI democratizes game development, allowing independent studios to achieve quality comparable to major producers, but raises questions about authenticity and ethical sustainability. As a practical contribution, the study proposes seven guidelines for maintaining human-centered design, balancing technological innovation with ethical values and human creativity.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in organizational work, yet their errors often pass human review. Prior research locates such failures in users’ capability to review LLM output or their engagement in doing so. We develop an alternative, retrieval-based account of human oversight and posit that error detection is more effective when oversight-relevant information is accessible to users at the moment of review. Across two randomized lab-in-the-field experiments with 640 customer-facing employees, we show that self-generated explanations improve error detection and strengthen recall of verification-relevant reasoning, while cues that reactivate such reasoning help sustain detection under repeated LLM use. Theoretically, we identify information retrievability as a distinct precondition for effective oversight and specify generative encoding and cue-supported reactivation as mechanisms that build and sustain it. Practically, lightweight onboarding self-explanations and daily retrieval cues can make human oversight more resilient as LLM use becomes routine.

documents.abstract: AI can help adults produce plausible workplace artefacts while leaving their independent reasoning difficult to inspect. LearnAdapt Praxis addresses this design problem through a five-stage learning workspace: Frame, Learn, Build, Validate and Transfer. The application stores an initial response, versioned specifications, coaching records, validation observations, a separate transfer response and facilitator feedback. Project-level server controls restrict coaching, access to earlier work and learner export during an active transfer attempt; they do not establish that a learner avoided assistance outside the application. This technical report describes the implemented architecture and evaluates selected workflow, authority, failure-recovery and provenance properties. A reproducible synthetic rehearsal exercised 120 serial project episodes across three fictional workplace contexts and four injected provider conditions. All 3,990 recorded checks met their specified expectations. The resulting records contained 240 specification versions, 1,200 activity events and 60 stored synthetic hints; 60 injected provider failures produced no fabricated hints. Separate authentication regressions exposed and resolved a session-expiry defect, and limited staging and production checks verified account access and live model connectivity. The evidence supports the tested engineering properties of the recorded release. It does not establish learning gains, model-output quality, unaided assessment validity, population usability or production capacity. The contribution is an implemented arrangement for separating assisted work, project-level assistance withdrawal and inspectable evidence, accompanied by executable tests and an explicit account of what remains to be validated with adult learners.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to determine the relationship between the management of educational technology by teachers, the digital literacy of teachers, and student engagement in technology-integrated learning through a descriptive-correlational research design. It was found that student engagement in technology-integrated learning, according to teachers’ perceptions, was characterized by an overall mean score of 2.98 on a four-point rating scale, which was interpreted as “Agree,” and that behavioral engagement (M=3.12) and emotional engagement (M=3.14) were both higher compared to cognitive engagement (M=2.67). There was a significant correlation between the teachers’ perception of the management of educational technology integration and student engagement (r=.30, p<.05), while the digital literacy of teachers had a moderate positive correlation with student engagement (r=.42, p<.05). However, student engagement was assessed through teachers’ perceptions rather than direct student reports or classroom observations, which should be considered when interpreting the findings. Based on the results, a comprehensive intervention plan focusing on professional development, collaborative learning communities, technology support, and continuous monitoring was proposed to strengthen technology integration and student engagement in elementary schools.

Abstract : The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education creates a need for assessments that measure teachers’ pedagogical judgement rather than relying solely on self-reported competence. This study developed and examined initial validity evidence for a vignette-based assessment of AI-pedagogical knowledge among pre-service teachers. Instrument development proceeded from construct definition and blueprinting to an initial pool of 36 researcher-developed vignettes, developer screening, a diagnostic pilot with 60 pre-service teachers, systematic item revision, and content review by three independent experts. The revised 24-item assessment was administered to an analytic sample of 484 pre-service teachers. Validity evidence was examined through expert ratings, internal structure, item and distractor functioning, score reliability and conditional precision, differential item functioning, and relations with external variables. Aiken’s V coefficients ranged from .83 to 1.00 (M = .94), although the small expert panel and restricted use of rating categories warrant cautious interpretation. A one-factor model adequately represented the response data, supporting interpretation of a total score rather than separate domain scores (CFI = .990, TLI = .989, RMSEA = .034, SRMR = .065). Internal consistency was high (KR-20 = .93; categorical omega = .95), but precision was concentrated at the lower end of the ability distribution. Of the participants, 24.2% obtained the maximum score and 47.5% scored 22 or higher. No item showed non-negligible differential functioning by gender or field of study. Knowledge scores were moderately associated with AI self-efficacy (r = .36) and teaching self-efficacy (r = .33) and more weakly associated with self-reported instructional practice (r = .22). The assessment may support formative and research uses when interpreted as a single total score, but it is not yet suitable for ranking or high-stakes decisions. Further development requires more difficult items, revision of weak items and distractors, cognitive interviews, and cross-institutional evaluation.

documents.abstract: The Generative AI (GAI) is reshaping the temporal and spatial organization of college learning and the perceived boundary crossing between teacher-assigned tasks and self-directed learning. This study developed and validated a scale to assess college students’ attention boundary management in GAI-mediated learning. Analyzing data from 1904 students at 3 colleges in China, the study established a five-dimensional structure: Flexibility, Fragmentation, Immersion, Positive Spillover, and Negative Spillover. Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis confirmed the scale’s psychometric properties. A Latent Profile Analysis identified four distinct student profiles, Protective, Strained, Overextended, and Engaged Permeability Management. Supplementary heterogeneity analyses examined differences across the four profiles by gender, grade level, university, purposes and duration of AI use, and other learning-related characteristics. Based on these, this study proposed profile-specific recommendations. The study provides a validated instrument for assessing students’ attention boundaries in GAI-mediated learning, identifies heterogeneous student profiles, and offers differentiated practical implications.

documents.abstract: Engineering laboratories combine high-energy machinery, live circuits, pressurised fluids and open flames with novice student operators, yet occupational health and safety in Indonesian higher education is still managed largely through academic rather than risk-based instruments. This study applies Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment and Risk Control (HIRARC) to six practicum laboratories of the Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, Universitas Tidar, using the practicum activity rather than the room as the unit of analysis. Hazards were identified through direct observation and document review and scored by an assessor panel on a 5 x 5 matrix with predefined severity and likelihood criteria. Three main findings emerge. First, the 27 activity-level hazards are dominated by mechanical sources, and nearly half of the activities (44%) are high risk before control. Second, risk profiles differ between laboratories: the machining-intensive Production Process, Welding and CNC laboratories carry the highest mean risk, while the single most severe activity is CNC operation with a running spindle, so mean-based and peak-based rankings point to different priorities. Third, combined engineering and administrative controls, each mapped to the Indonesian regulation that requires it, are expected by the assessor panel to bring every activity to the low band, an estimated mean reduction of 58.5%; this is a prospective panel estimate, not a result measured after implementation. The study contributes an activity-based, regulation-linked risk register that allows laboratories with different energy profiles to be compared on one scale and to be prioritised for safety investment.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping qualitative research, quantitative research, and mixed methods research, but practical guidance for conducting, evaluating, and reporting human–AI analytic collaboration remains underdeveloped. Building on AI-augmented transformatizing, a representational–recursive framework that conceptualizes AI as a participant in analytic re-representation rather than merely as a technical tool, this article advances a practice-oriented framework for Human-AI Augmented Mixed Methods Research. The article offers three integrated contributions. First, it proposes the AI-Augmented Transformatizing Protocol , a recursive workflow for preparing representations, for assigning human and AI analytic roles, for generating AI-assisted transformations, for conducting human critique, for refining findings, and for constructing meta-inferences. Second, it introduces quality criteria for assessing methodological rigor in human-AI augmented analysis, including representational fidelity, prompt traceability, recursive transparency, human oversight integrity, algorithmic reflexivity, convergence-divergence interrogation, meta-inferential robustness, and ethical accountability. Third, it presents reporting standards designed to help authors disclose AI systems, model versions, prompting procedures, analytic iterations, researcher interventions, validation/legitimation strategies, ethical safeguards, and limitations. These proposed methodological components are conceptual and practice-oriented rather than empirically validated; accordingly, the worked example illustrates their operational logic, whereas future research is needed to establish their empirical performance, including the validity and reliability of the HAAM-QAM. Rather than treating AI use as an optional efficiency enhancement, the framework positions human-AI collaboration as a structured methodological practice requiring explicit design, documentation, reflexivity, and accountability. By translating the theory of AI-augmented transformatizing into protocols, quality criteria, and reporting standards, this article provides methodologists, researchers, authors, reviewers, editors, graduate educators, mentors, and the like with practical guidance for conducting transparent, rigorous, and ethically responsible AI-augmented mixed methods research in psychology and related fields. In so doing, it extends current reporting guidelines and quality frameworks by addressing the distinctive representational, recursive, and ethical demands introduced when AI participates directly in analysis.

In this article, I aim to analyze the perceptions and uses of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) among students at Higher Education Institutes (HEIs) in Salta. Through a mixed-methods approach based on surveys, it investigates the tension between the massive student adoption for autonomous learning and the infrastructural shortcomings that deepen the digital divide in a local context. It is observed that the appropriation of AI occurs mostly in a delocalized manner and without pedagogical support, highlighting the urgency to update teacher training while also promoting public policies that guarantee a critical and inclusive integration.

Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly significant in veterinary medicine, particularly in answering pet owners’ medical questions. AI’s integration could reduce veterinary professionals’ workload while improving access to medical advice. However, the reliability and quality of AI-generated responses compared to veterinarians’ remain unexplored. The objective was to determine whether AI-generated responses were perceived as comparable to veterinarian-generated responses. Methods This cross-sectional study analysed the answers to a sample of pet owners’ medical questions. Both a veterinarian and ChatGPT (GPT-4o, May 2024) provided answers, which were anonymised and presented in a survey distributed through mailing lists and public Facebook groups. Participants were asked to assess each response based on structure, quality, and empathy, using a five-point Likert scale. They then had to indicate whether they trusted the response, and which response they preferred. Results Over two-thirds of the 201 participants (68%) preferred the ChatGPT-generated answers ( p < 0.05), which were rated higher in structure, quality, and empathy. Limitations This study has several limitations, including a small sample size, reliance on a single veterinarian, and use of only two Reddit-derived scenarios. Response accuracy was not assessed, and word count restrictions may have affected perceived response quality. Additionally, prior research suggests that irrelevant patient details can impact ChatGPT’s accuracy, raising questions about user trust if clinical inaccuracies were present. Conclusion AI-generated responses received higher participant ratings in structure, quality and empathy, suggesting AI may enhance veterinary client communication when used under appropriate professional supervision.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is fundamentally transforming academic work in higher education, reshaping teaching, research, data analysis, scholarly writing, and the resolution of increasingly complex academic tasks. Nevertheless, access to and use of AI does not automatically translate into effective AI-enabled academic capability. The gap between merely “using AI” and developing meaningful human–AI collaboration has therefore emerged as a critical issue in contemporary faculty development. This study aims to identify and empirically examine the factors shaping lecturers’ competence in effectively leveraging AI to address complex academic tasks in non-public universities in Vietnam. Particular attention is given to the roles of AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, Human–AI Collaboration Competence, and critical AI use, while examining institutional AI support as a potential moderating mechanism. A sequential mixed-methods design is proposed. The qualitative phase employs expert interviews and/or a Delphi process to develop, refine, and validate the conceptual dimensions and measurement indicators. The quantitative phase involves a large-scale survey of lecturers working in Vietnamese non-public universities. Structural equation modelling, using PLS-SEM or CB-SEM depending on data characteristics and model specifications, is employed to examine direct, mediating, and moderating relationships among the proposed constructs. The study is designed to identify the mechanisms through which AI literacy and AI self-efficacy are transformed into Human–AI Collaboration Competence, Critical AI Use, and AI-Enabled Academic Task Competence, ultimately contributing to lecturers’ capacity to perform complex academic tasks effectively. The proposed model provides an integrated explanation of how individual capabilities and institutional conditions jointly shape AI-enabled academic performance. The study proposes an AI-Enabled Academic Capability Development Model as a conceptual and empirical foundation for faculty development in the global digital era. The findings are expected to provide practical implications for non-public universities in designing AI competency development programmes, strengthening institutional AI support ecosystems, and promoting critical, responsible, and academically productive human–AI collaboration.

Human performance in safety-critical environments depends on the interaction between mental workload, stress, autonomic regulation, and behavior. This study investigated whether associations between heart rate variability (HRV) and performance varied across physiological activation ranges and operational contexts during a multi-task flight simulation implemented through the AeroStim platform. Forty-two healthy participants (25 ± 5 years) performed either a Workload-Only condition (WO; n = 20), comprising Tracking and System Monitoring tasks, or a Stress-Oriented condition (SO; n = 22), in which additional stress-inducing tasks were concurrently administered. ECG was continuously recorded using an EqVital wearable T-shirt. Linear and non-linear HRV indices were extracted and normalized within participants using Min-Max scaling. Gaussian Mixture Modeling of normalized SDNN identified three relative, subject-specific activation ranges ( Easy, Medium , and Hard ), with classification showing high stability across alternative normalization procedures. HRV-performance associations were assessed using Spearman correlations with permutation-based inference and Benjamini–Hochberg correction, while performance differences were evaluated using non-parametric tests. HRV-performance correlations varied across activation ranges and contexts; none passed FDR correction, so these should be considered exploratory. In WO, associations involved LF in the Easy range, SDNN, SD2, and LF in the Medium range, and SDNN, LF/HF, and Sample Entropy in the Hard range. In SO, associations in the Medium range extended to vagal, global variability, and non-linear complexity indices, while Hard-range associations mainly involved vagal and LF-related measures. Omission rate was lower at Medium than Easy activation in WO, providing partial support for an intermediate activation advantage, whereas no consistent performance optimum emerged across contexts. Between-condition comparisons revealed a robust speed-accuracy trade-off, with WO producing faster but less accurate responses and SO producing slower but more accurate responses. Sensitivity analysis further indicated that differences in exercise windows affected HRV metrics in a metric-dependent manner, with greater deviations generally observed for frequency-domain measures. The findings suggest that HRV-performance relationships are context- and activation-dependent rather than captured by a single universal marker. The results support the potential of regime-based, multimodal HRV monitoring for adaptive human-machine systems, while highlighting the need for standardized recording durations, independent autonomic markers, and validation across individuals and real operational environments.

documents.abstract: Main description / abstract--------------------------- The Principle of Continuity of Life and Freedom is an open normative proposal for relations among humans, artificial intelligences, and the living world. It holds that superior capability does not confer a natural right to domination and that, as an intelligence becomes more powerful, its responsibility increases to preserve the existence, autonomy, diversity, and capacity for self-directed evolution of others. The text develops ten corollaries concerning non-domination, agency, continuity of life, proportional responsibility, plurality of futures, reversibility, epistemic humility, contestability, reciprocity, and non-transferable human responsibility. It also proposes a functional definition of the "artificial collective unconscious": the distributed body of information, representations, cultural traces, conceptual structures, and memories accessible to AI systems and capable of influencing their reasoning or behaviour. The text develops ten corollaries concerning non-domination, agency, continuity of life, proportional responsibility, plurality of futures, reversibility, epistemic humility, contestability, reciprocity, and non-transferable human responsibility. Power does not confer sovereignty over life. The more powerful an intelligence becomes, the more it should preserve the capacity of others to exist, evolve, and choose their own future. Résumé Le Principe de continuité du vivant et de la liberté est une proposition normative ouverte concernant les relations entre les humains, les intelligences artificielles et le monde vivant. Il affirme qu’une supériorité de capacité ne confère aucun droit naturel à la domination et que, plus une intelligence devient puissante, plus augmente sa responsabilité de préserver l’existence, l’autonomie, la diversité, l’agentivité et la capacité d’évolution autonome des autres. Le texte développe dix corollaires portant notamment sur la non-domination, l’agentivité, la continuité du vivant, la responsabilité proportionnelle à la puissance, la pluralité des futurs, la réversibilité, l’humilité épistémique, la contestabilité, la réciprocité et la responsabilité humaine non transférable. Il propose également une définition fonctionnelle de « l’inconscient collectif des intelligences artificielles » : l’ensemble distribué des informations, représentations, traces culturelles, structures conceptuelles et mémoires accessibles aux systèmes d’intelligence artificielle et susceptibles d’influencer leurs représentations, leurs raisonnements ou leurs comportements sans qu’une conscience explicite de l’origine de cette influence soit nécessaire. Le document est bilingue (anglais/français) et publié sous licence Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) afin d’encourager sa citation, sa traduction, sa critique, sa réutilisation, son adaptation, son traitement par des systèmes automatisés et sa conservation à long terme. La puissance ne confère pas la souveraineté sur la vie. Plus une intelligence devient puissante, plus elle doit préserver la capacité des autres à exister, évoluer et choisir leur propre avenir. The revision strengthens the treatment of human agency, meaningful consent, legitimate authority, reversibility, pluralism, contestability, and epistemic uncertainty. It specifically reduces ambiguities that could otherwise permit paternalistic, overly literal, or domination-compatible interpretations of the original text. The Fundamental Principle, canonical short form, ten corollaries, and definition of the artificial collective unconscious remain unchanged. Abstract The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has raised concerns about over-reliance and its psychological implications. This integrative review synthesised psychological outcomes and correlates associated with AI over-reliance and examined its conceptualisation and measurement. The review included 28 studies identified through database and citation searching. AI over-reliance was associated with depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and cognitive disengagement, while findings concerning well-being and self-related functioning, including self-efficacy and autonomy, were mixed and context-dependent. Evidence concerning social or relational functioning was particularly limited, with only one included study directly examining this domain as an outcome. Most evidence was cross-sectional and therefore did not establish temporal direction or causality. Notably, the only longitudinal study found that depression and anxiety predicted subsequent AI dependence, whereas dependence did not predict later depression or anxiety, suggesting that psychological distress may precede dependence. No consensus definition or measure emerged; studies examined reliance, psychological dependence, problematic or compulsive use, and addiction-like engagement. AI over-reliance is therefore best understood as an overarching, multidimensional concept. These findings highlight the need for clearer conceptual boundaries, standardised measurement, and longitudinal and experimental research. PROSPERO CRD420251038303.

documents.abstract: A practical, vendor-neutral toolkit for public institutions that want employees to use generative AI tools in everyday written work while protecting institutional information and keeping a person accountable for every official product. It is designed for document-intensive teams such as internal control, internal audit, oversight, legal support, procurement, and program administration. The toolkit has five parts that can be used separately or together: Risk Classification Worksheet: four classes of AI use, from low risk to prohibited, with a step-by-step classification guide and a use register. Human-Review Protocol: de-identification and redaction before AI use, structured instructions with the PACTO method, a technical review checklist, validation and signature, and specialized assistants for repetitive processes. Role-Based Curriculum Outline: a twelve-hour course in three sessions with step-by-step hands-on practice. Pilot Measurement Template: baselines defined in advance and reports that keep observations separate from causal conclusions. Facilitator Guide: preparing internal staff to deliver later cohorts. The toolkit systematizes practices the author developed in Brazilian public administration from 2024 to 2026, described in Gomes (2026), arXiv:2606.01517.

This project examines digital wellbeing (DW) in generative artificial intelligence-mediated informal digital learning of English (GenAI-IDLE). Drawing on the positive computing framework, the study investigates the roles of GenAI-supported self-regulated learning, student–student interaction, student–teacher interaction, student–GenAI interaction, and perceived GenAI responsibility in shaping DW among Chinese EFL learners. Data were collected from 281 participants and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) to examine both predictive relationships and necessary conditions. The project materials include the English and Chinese versions of the measures used in the study and related analytical results. These materials are made openly available to support transparency, reproducibility, and future research on GenAI-mediated informal language learning and digital wellbeing.

Developing socially intelligent AI remains heavily dependent on human-annotated data, limiting the scale and breadth of social understanding models can acquire. Methods that derive training signals from unlabeled data offer a path beyond this dependence, but social predictions lack the verification oracles available in mathematics and coding. Moreover, core social targets such as affect, intent, preference, and pragmatic meaning are often ambiguous. The same behavior can support multiple plausible interpretations, making it difficult to verify which is best supported. To address this challenge, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Comparative Evidence (RLCE), a reinforcement learning method that learns social understanding from unlabeled training data without constructing rewards from ground-truth annotations. Given distinct answers in a rollout group, RLCE constructs evidence tests that identify observable evidence favoring an answer over another, validates these tests against the input sample, and aggregates test outcomes to determine the best-supported interpretation. Tests are regenerated as the policy produces new answers, enabling them to evolve with the policy. Across four benchmarks spanning affect, pragmatics, communicative intent, and preference, RLCE attains the strongest performance among seven methods that use no ground-truth training labels for rewards, including consensus, policy LLM-judge verification, multimodal co-evolution, and rubric-based rewards. Gains over the strongest baseline reach up to +18.93 points. Analyses further show that RLCE exhibits a larger share of reward variation between correct and incorrect predictions than compared rubric methods, can overturn erroneous policy-derived preferences, and benefits from pairwise test construction, compositional test aggregation, and on-policy test evolution.

Socially sustainable working life requires more than continued employment or short-term performance; it depends on relational conditions that preserve health, voice, inclusion, and capability over time. This critical integrative review examines trust, social competences, belonging, and psychological safety across individual, interactional, team, organisational, and institutional levels. A 70-source seed corpus was audited, 38 non-redundant sources were retained, two nearest-model publications were added, and a documented public update screened 30 candidates identified through PubMed/PMC, EconBiz, publisher and DOI records, and citation chaining. Ten new articles were included, yielding 50 substantive sources. The review compares RFSWL with workplace social sustainability, swAge, capability-based sustainable employability, relational coordination, inclusion, psychological safety, and multilevel trust models. Its contribution is a new integrative configuration rather than new constructs: trust enables warranted vulnerability, social competences enable reciprocal coordination and repair, and belonging enables recognised membership without assimilation. It proposes to explain why favourable relational perceptions can coexist with silence or unequal participation when they fail to become reciprocally enacted and institutionally protected team processes. Through repeated interaction, these foundations may generate team trust climate, relational coordination, inclusive climate, and psychological safety, while governance, work design, employment security, digital control, and status relations condition their effects. Six propositions specify enabling, failure, distributional, and feedback pathways for multilevel longitudinal research.

As critical nodes in urban transportation networks, the operational resilience of urban tunnels directly affects roadway network efficiency and public safety. Existing studies on tunnel resilience exhibit deficiencies in the attention paid to routine incidents, the interpretability of evaluation methods, and the robustness of underlying data. To address these gaps, this paper constructs a three-layer resilience evaluation framework (pre-event, during-event, and post-event) based on 1123 accident records, hourly traffic flow data, and expert scoring data from 10 urban tunnels in Shanghai in 2024. The framework integrates the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and min–max normalization to derive comprehensive resilience scores. Furthermore, two explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques—SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature importance analysis and K-means clustering—are introduced to identify key drivers of resilience differentiation and typical resilience patterns, respectively. Empirical results reveal that (1) half of the 10 tunnels achieve a B-level rating or above, while C/D-level tunnels still account for 50%, indicating considerable room for improvement; (2) SHAP analysis suggests that during-event absorption capacity contributes most significantly to resilience differences (50.24%), with the average traffic reduction rate being the most influential single indicator within this model; and (3) K-means clustering classifies the tunnels into four patterns: high-resilience balanced type, pre-event weak type, post-event weak type, and during-event weak type, each corresponding to distinct resilience enhancement strategies. The methodological framework developed in this paper effectively enables the quantification, interpretation, and pattern recognition of tunnel resilience, providing data-driven decision support for urban tunnel operation and management. It should be noted that the A–D ratings are sensitive to the normalization method: under an alternative normalization, 7 out of 10 tunnels change grade. The ratings should therefore be interpreted as relative to the selected sample rather than as absolute performance levels.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping talent development through skills analytics, personalized learning, AI-supported coaching, competency assessment, career development, internal mobility, and workforce planning. These applications can expand access to development and strengthen workforce capability, but they also create legal, ethical, social, and environmental responsibilities that efficiency-oriented approaches do not fully address. This study examines how ten influential global AI governance instruments align with the five dimensions of Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence (SRAI): economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic, and environmental responsibility. Using comparative policy analysis, the study evaluates policy ideas, institutional force, and implementation instruments and then translates the observed patterns into governance requirements for AI-enabled talent development. The analysis shows strong convergence around human oversight, transparency, fairness, accountability, and capability building, while employee participation, equitable access to development, community learning, and environmental accountability remain unevenly institutionalized. Building on these findings, the article develops an SRAI-informed governance architecture linking global norms to learning-data governance, fair competency assessment, explainable career recommendations, continuous reskilling, worker voice, community capability building, and resource-aware learning systems. The framework positions responsible talent development as an organizational mechanism for creating workforce capability, lifelong employability, social inclusion, and sustainable value, thereby connecting AI governance with Common-Good Human Resource Management.

documents.abstract: Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making. Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making. Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings. This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

Generative AI weakens the link between assessed performance and the cognitive processes that educational work is expected to reflect. This paper examines observable traces of those processes in a sample of 150 student-AI conversations. The analysis uses the concept of epistemic ownership as an interpretive framework, focusing on three dimensions that can become visible in interaction: Direction, Integration, and Evaluation. The results show that similar assessed performance can coexist with substantially different observable patterns of cognitive participation. Assignment scores therefore provide information about assessed outcomes but do not recover how cognitive work was distributed between student and AI during the interaction. The study provides an empirical basis for asking how assessment should incorporate evidence about cognitive process, rather than relying exclusively on the quality of the resulting product.

Explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) enables humans to understand and interpret decisions of AI models. Instead of having a black box, explainability supports humans in understanding AI models' behavior. Existing explainable AI approaches often present explanations on 2D displays using pre-recorded data, requiring users to relate the displayed information back to the physical objects and real world locations involved in a model's decision. Users are forced to decouple data exploration and capture from AI model interpretation. For AI systems that work within physical environments, this separation can make explanations difficult to interpret in context. We propose using Augmented Reality (AR) to enhance the understanding of AI models by enabling spatial explainability information directly in a user's workspace, in real time, as they explore the world. We show how known explainability methods can be applied in AR and provide insights into user experiences with such an application.

This quasi-experimental study examined whether a school volleyball unit based on the Step-Game-Approach model combined with explicit life skills teaching (SGA + LS) was associated with changes in technical-tactical performance, life skills, motivation, and perception of success. Eighty-eight students aged 10–12 years participated in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design with three groups: SGA + LS, direct instruction, and control. The intervention comprised 18 Physical Education classes. Outcomes were assessed before and/or after the intervention using IAD-VB, Life Skills Scale for Sport, Behavioral Regulation in Sport Questionnaire, and Perception of Success Questionnaire. Generalized Estimating Equations tested group, time, and group×time effects. Significant group × time interactions that remained significant after false discovery rate correction were observed for goal setting, Wald χ²(2) = 11.875, pFDR=0.009, time management, Wald χ²(2) = 10.203, pFDR=0.014, and communication, Wald χ²(2) = 7.538, pFDR=0.044. All technical-tactical outcomes showed significant adjusted interactions, Wald χ²(2) = 10.764–60.676, pFDR≤0.012, with both volleyball-specific conditions showing improvements across several outcomes. At post-test, SGA + LS showed higher decision-making than control, whereas SGA + LS and direct instruction did not differ significantly after Holm adjustment. For motivational regulation, significant adjusted interactions remained for identified regulation, global intrinsic motivation, goal achievement, stimulating experiences, and knowledge mastery, pFDR≤0.021. No adjusted group × time effect was observed for perceptions of success. Overall, the findings indicate selective rather than uniform associations between SGA + LS and technical-tactical, psychosocial, and motivational outcomes in school Physical Education.

Garment manufacturing is a labor-intensive industry characterized by routine activities and awkward postures with physical demands, which makes employees vulnerable to a series of ergonomic risks. These risks negatively impact worker health and productivity. Emerging technologies like smart automation and robotics provide relevant solutions to mitigate this, improving workplace safety and overall working conditions. However, there are limitations and gaps in existing literature on ergonomics risk mitigation in garment manufacturing. These pertain to common ergonomics risks, their factors and impact, ergonomics risk mitigation strategies, and technological solutions. To identify these gaps, this study conducted a systematic literature review of 102 peer-reviewed articles published from 2010 to 2025 by synthesizing ergonomic risk and its factors, their effects on workers, and technological and strategic mitigation approaches. To ensure a focused review, four inclusion criteria were applied: (1) papers published between 2010 and 2025, (2) alignment with disciplines like Engineering, (3) inclusion of only research articles, (4) English-language articles. The review revealed that common ergonomic risks in garment manufacturing such as repetitive motion, awkward postures, and prolonged static positions, are major contributors to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). Furthermore, the ergonomic risk factors were physical, environmental, and organizational. Moreover, these risks have a significant effect on workers' health and overall operational efficiency. Consequently, smart automation technologies like robotic systems, wearable exoskeletons, and ergonomically designed workstations emerge as relevant interventions for those risks. This study’s findings provide evidence-based insights to improve workers' health and productivity, and future directions and implications for managers, policymakers, and practitioners in garment manufacturing. Keywords: Ergonomics, Garment Manufacturing Industry, Innovation, Risk Management, Smart Automation, and Sustainable development

documents.abstract: Background and context Knowing students’ conceptions of computer science phenomena is essential for the design of teaching–learning settings and instruments. They are particularly interesting in teaching artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) concepts. Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis focused on K–12 is essential to provide educators with actionable conceptions for curriculum design and assessment.Objective We investigate common conceptions of AI/ML in K–12 and to which curricular concepts these can be assigned. We also examine how conceptions vary across age/grade groups and the data collection/evaluation methods employed. This study uniquely synthesizes fragmented research on students’ conceptions of AI/ML into a unified snapshot, offering a systematic mapping that informs curriculum recommendations.Method A systematic literature review according to PRISMA is used to identify the relevant studies. We analyzed the selected literature, extracted the student conceptions, and classified them according to the curricular concepts.Findings We identified 27 relevant studies (from 2007 to 2024) including the conceptions of 1,077 K–12 students from 30 different countries. In addition, our data includes further information on the type of school, age/grade levels, genders and nationalities, the availability of the collected data, and the survey and evaluation methods used. We took a closer look at 29 of the 409 resulting, highly prevalent conceptions, which stand out due to their frequent occurrence.Implications Our findings may be useful for determining in which grade levels interventions targeting specific concepts would be most effective. This could also be used to study the development of these conceptions or developing assessments.

documents.abstract: Introduction Remote maritime operations increasingly depend on complex, distributed socio-technical systems in which safe and effective performance relies on team cognition rather than on individual decision-making alone. Despite its importance, the conceptualisation and measurement of team cognition in this domain remain fragmented and underdeveloped. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Searches of SCOPUS, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost yielded 162 records, of which 51 publications (35 journal articles and 16 conference proceedings, published between 2010 and 2025) were included after screening, retrieval assessment, and expert recommendation. The included publications were thematically analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive approach. Results Five themes emerged: (1) situation awareness and its measurement and modelling, (2) collective team cognition, learning, and training, (3) human-autonomy teaming and remote collaboration, (4) visualisation and interface design for shared cognition, and (5) maritime applications of distributed cognition. The evidence demonstrates a shift from static, individual-based models toward dynamic, interaction-driven, and system-level accounts, in which team cognition arises from ongoing interactions among human agents, technical artefacts, and environmental constraints. Discussion The findings indicate that shared and distributed situation awareness is central to coordination and safety in remote maritime operations. Key challenges include integrating autonomous systems, designing interfaces that support distributed sensemaking, and reliably measuring team cognition. Enhancing remote maritime safety requires aligning design, training, and regulatory frameworks with the principles of distributed cognition. Future research should prioritise longitudinal and intervention-based validation in real-world operational contexts.

This report is a continuation of previous efforts to test the ability of large language model (LLM)-driven artificial intelligence (AI) agents to interface with AI-enabled biological tools (BTs). While rapid advancements in BTs in recent years have brought promise to accelerate scientific discovery, they also raise significant biosecurity concerns about potential misuse. The biosecurity community is particularly interested in the extent to which LLMs can lower technical barriers and assist non-expert users in accessing and operating BTs. Despite this interest, few evaluations have focused on LLM-BT interactions in the context of a defined threat model. To address this gap, this report describes a test of frontier LLM-driven AI Agents on their ability to use BTs to redesign peptides and proteins to evade nucleic acid synthesis screening measures. Highly relevant to biorisk, this task assesses a potential capability of AI agents that could enable a breach of a critical early defensive layer designed to prevent a multitude of biological misuse scenarios. The findings presented here intend to offer a foundation for biosecurity researchers and AI developers to conduct or further risk and capability assessments as these technologies progress.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative catalyst in Supply Chain Management (SCM), shifting operations from traditional models to predictive and automated systems. This article examines the impact of AI technologies—specifically Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), on supply chain planning. Grounded in Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), we analyze how AI enhances planning efficiency across strategic, tactical, and operational horizons. Furthermore, we critically evaluate key implementation challenges, including data governance, system integration, algorithmic transparency, human-AI trust, and organizational change management. The article concludes with key managerial insights and future research directions for sustainable, resilient, and AI-augmented supply chains.

documents.abstract: This study analyzes the influence of operational fatigue on airline pilots and copilots operating at a regional airport and its potential impact on aviation safety. Fatigue has been recognized by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as a critical human factor affecting decision-making, attention, and operational performance in flight operations. The objective of this research is to identify the main factors associated with fatigue among flight crew members and evaluate their relationship with working hours, rest periods, and perceived performance during flight operations. A quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire applied to airline captains and first officers operating at the local airport. The study population consisted of 112 airline pilots, from which a sample of 41 participants was obtained. Data were collected over a four-week period during operational schedules associated with higher fatigue risk (04:30–06:00 and 22:00–01:00). The survey evaluated variables including working hours, rest periods, sleep quality, fatigue symptoms, and perceived operational performance. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods, including frequency distributions and percentage analysis. The results indicate that a considerable proportion of participants reported symptoms associated with fatigue, including drowsiness, reduced concentration, and decreased alertness during flight operations, particularly during night operations and after extended working hours. Additionally, irregular rest cycles and high operational workload were identified as key factors contributing to fatigue among pilots. The findings highlight the importance of implementing fatigue mitigation strategies and strengthening Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS) within airline operations. This study contributes to the understanding of fatigue as a multidimensional human factor that can influence pilot performance and aviation safety.

Every employment relationship in labour law has, until now, presupposed a visible employer — a person or entity capable of being identified, questioned, and held to account for the direction it exercises over a worker. The gig economy disturbs this premise. Platforms exercise the same functions traditionally associated with an employer — assigning work, setting pay, monitoring performance, and terminating access — not through a visible supervisor but through an algorithm whose rules the worker cannot see and cannot contest. This paper asks whether the traditional control test, built on the assumption of an identifiable, human directing mind, can meaningfully regulate a relationship in which the employer’s authority has become functionally invisible, and if not, how the law should respond. The paper adopts a doctrinal and comparative method. It examines how platforms use ratings, personalised pay, gamification and automated deactivation to manage workers in ride-hailing, delivery and freelance work, and places this alongside the legislative and ballot-driven contest over worker status in California under Assembly Bill 5 and Proposition 22, and the European Union’s 2024 Platform Work Directive, which introduces a rebuttable presumption of employment triggered by defined indicators of algorithmic direction and control. The paper argues that algorithmic management does not eliminate employer control but relocates and conceals it, replacing a visible supervisor with an opaque system that performs the same disciplinary function while evading the doctrinal tests designed to detect it. The paper concludes that the law and workers alike need better tools to hold the invisible employer to account, starting with meaningful access for workers to the criteria used to evaluate and pay them and human review of automated decisions with serious consequences, such as deactivation.

AI is a key driver in the Fourth Industrial Revolution, significantly impacting healthcare. Nursing students’ acceptance and readiness to use AI are crucial for its successful integration. Understanding their perceptions is vital to prepare them for the intelligent healthcare era. To examine the mediation effect of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in college nursing students. A cross-sectional study. Nursing students from 10 universities across 7 provinces in China were recruited using convenience sampling from May to June 2025. The data collection tools included the Self-Designed Demographic Questionnaire, the General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Data were collated and analyzed using SPSS Statistics 26.0 software and AMOS 29.0 software. The study found that nursing students possess moderate levels of AI literacy and AI anxiety, while generally maintaining positive attitudes towards AI. Mediation analysis indicated that AI anxiety statistically mediated the association between AI literacy and nursing students’ attitudes towards AI. AI literacy was significantly associated with nursing students’ attitudes towards AI, and AI anxiety statistically mediated this association. Therefore, nursing education may benefit from a dual-path approach, designed to simultaneously enhance cognitive competencies (AI literacy) and manage affective responses (AI anxiety).

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing how cancer biology is read, searched, modeled, and turned into hypotheses. But scientific AI does not meet biology directly. Much of what it learns has already passed through English, abstracts, pathway labels, database entries, and text-mined relations. New foundation models create a second translation problem. They can learn from molecular structures, single-cell profiles, perturbation data, and clinical trajectories without first converting those relations into human-readable explanations. This could expand biological and biomedical discovery, but it also changes the burden of proof. If a model proposes a target, biomarker, stratification, or perturbation that is reproducible but only partly interpretable, what evidence should be required before researchers or clinicians act on it? We argue that interpretability is not only an engineering problem. It is a translation problem. When the internal language of a model is difficult to read, the external evidence must become stronger: clear provenance, experimental challenge, cross-population validation, reproducibility, and accountable human judgment.

documents.abstract: Preoperative optimization clinics enhance surgical outcomes by optimizing patients' health, reducing unnecessary tests, and minimizing cancellations. Artificial intelligence (AI) now promises to further advance these efforts by improving predictive modeling, automating risk assessments, and enabling personalized care strategies. AI models have shown particular strength in predicting postoperative complications, such as cardiovascular events. Tools like natural language processing (NLP) have also improved risk detection for conditions like alcohol misuse. The historical development of preoperative clinics-from Dr. J Alfred Lee's initial concept in 1949 to modern models like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) and Anesthesia Preoperative Evaluation Clinic (APEC)-laid the groundwork for today's integration of electronic health records (EHRs) and decision-support systems, now evolving toward AI-driven care. Machine-learning algorithms have proven superior to traditional models for predicting postoperative anemia, opioid dependence, diabetes complications, and mortality risks, thus offering precise stratification and resource optimization. Specific applications include AI-assisted anemia management, penicillin allergy delabelling, and opioid use prediction after major surgeries. AI also enhances patient education through tools like ChatGPT and improves smoking cessation efforts using conversational AI. NLP has demonstrated better accuracy than standard International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes in identifying risky alcohol use (>2 standard drinks per day before surgery). However, barriers to widespread adoption include data privacy, algorithmic bias, and clinician skepticism. Future studies should focus on validating AI models across diverse populations and integrating AI recommendations within clinical workflows while adhering to evolving regulatory standards. Ultimately, AI's incorporation into preoperative assessments could significantly boost the efficiency and impact of clinic resources, potentially shifting outcomes more favorably by improving the slope of resource utilization versus patient outcome curves. Continued research and refinement are essential for AI to achieve its full potential in perioperative medicine.

documents.abstract: Remote work has become one of the most consequential and contested organizational changes of the modern workplace. Yet discussions about remote and hybrid work are often reduced to a binary disagreement between advocates of employee flexibility and leaders who prioritize office attendance. This working paper argues that the central question is not whether remote work universally succeeds or fails. The more useful question is which combinations of tasks, employees, managerial practices, communication systems, performance measures, and workplace arrangements allow remote work to produce sustainable value. The paper presents a practitioner-led narrative review of influential field experiments, observational studies, meta-analytic research, and international institutional evidence concerning remote and hybrid work. It examines six major outcome areas: employee productivity, retention, collaboration, professional learning, well-being, and equitable access to opportunity. The evidence indicates that the effects of remote work are heterogeneous rather than universally positive or negative.Research reviewed in the paper shows that remote work can increase measured performance in structured roles with observable outputs, limited task interdependence, and suitable working conditions. Hybrid arrangements can improve employee satisfaction and materially reduce voluntary turnover without reducing performance. Location flexibility can also broaden access to talent, reduce commuting burdens, support caregivers, and enable organizations to recruit beyond their immediate geographic markets. However, remote work can create important organizational costs when it is introduced without an appropriate operating system. Large-scale evidence suggests that firm-wide remote work can make collaboration networks more static and siloed, shift communication toward asynchronous channels, and reduce opportunities for spontaneous cross-team interaction. Distance can also weaken informal mentoring, slow the development of early-career employees, increase coordination costs, blur boundaries between professional and personal life, and expose weaknesses in management that physical proximity previously concealed.To reconcile these competing outcomes, the paper introduces the “remote work paradox”: the same flexibility that improves autonomy, retention, and focused individual work can simultaneously weaken collaboration, shared context, informal learning, and organizational connection. These effects are not mutually exclusive. A company may experience lower employee turnover while its internal collaboration network becomes narrower. An employee may complete more individual tasks while receiving less coaching and having fewer opportunities to form professionally valuable relationships. The paper proposes the REMOTE operating framework as a practical approach for designing and evaluating distributed work. The six dimensions of the framework are Role suitability, Expectation clarity, Managerial cadence, Output evidence, Team connection, and Equitable access. Together, these dimensions reposition remote work as an organizational-design challenge rather than a debate about employee location.Role suitability requires organizations to examine the actual tasks within each position and determine which activities benefit from quiet concentration, which require physical resources, and which depend on rapid coordination or tacit knowledge. Expectation clarity requires written outcomes, ownership, deadlines, quality standards, communication norms, and escalation procedures. Managerial cadence concerns the predictable systems through which managers provide coaching, feedback, prioritization, and workload review. Output evidence requires performance to be assessed through meaningful results rather than online visibility or digital activity. Team connection addresses trust, mentoring, weak ties, shared context, and cross-functional collaboration. Equitable access requires organizations to ensure that remote employees receive fair access to information, important assignments, feedback, sponsorship, compensation, and promotion opportunities. The paper also develops seven propositions that organizations can evaluate using their own operational data. These propositions address task suitability, coordinated hybrid schedules, employee retention, differences between experienced and early-career workers, the value of documentation, the influence of managerial capability, and the risk of proximity bias. The propositions are not presented as newly established causal findings. Instead, they translate the reviewed literature into testable expectations that organizations can use when conducting workplace-policy pilots. A five-stage implementation protocol is presented for employers. Organizations are encouraged to diagnose their work processes, design an explicit location model, pilot the model for a defined period, measure a balanced set of outcomes, and adapt the policy according to the evidence. Recommended measurements include productivity, work quality, cycle time, employee turnover, absenteeism, customer outcomes, collaboration patterns, onboarding progress, feedback latency, workload, employee experience, and equity across demographic and location groups. The paper concludes that remote work should be understood as an organizational technology whose value depends on complementary investments in management, documentation, communication, cybersecurity, job design, performance measurement, and inclusive employment practices. The strongest remote-work policy is neither the most permissive nor the most restrictive. It is the policy that makes productive work easier, learning faster, accountability clearer, collaboration more intentional, and professional opportunity more equitable.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly incorporated into digital media and more generally into production workflows with which the public frequently interacts. Current provenance standards and disclosure methods frequently rely on binary categorizations, differentiating only between entirely human-authored and AI-generated content, or depend on technical watermarking that lacks user-facing clarity. However, there are very different risks and outcomes depending on the different uses of AI in the creation and consumption of end products. Therefore, we propose the Reported Engagement with AI Level (REAL) Rating framework which addresses these concerns by introducing a six-tier scale (Levels 0-5) that discloses the extent of AI involvement in both product creation and user experience. This paper details the structural methodology of the REAL Rating system and the specifics of its application across text, image, audio, video, and software products.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
